summary: Collects the most critical operational considerations for deploying BGP origin validation based on RPKI. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Origin validation uses the RPKI, a database of certificates that says which autonomous system is allowed to announce which prefix, to check BGP announcements. This document lists what an operator has to get right: where the data comes from, how fresh it is, and how the three possible answers, Valid, NotFound and Invalid, should be treated in routing policy.

questions: what is a roa max length
subtitle: How to run BGP origin validation based on the RPKI without breaking the routes you rely on.

tldr.problem: Origin validation checks that a network is allowed to announce a prefix, but deploying it touches caching, clocks, trust anchors and routing policy, and a mistake there can make reachable prefixes unreachable.
tldr.mechanism: The document collects the operational rules: publish hierarchical repositories, distribute validated caches, keep router clocks right, and set routing policy so that Valid is preferred, NotFound is still used, and Invalid is dropped.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7115 is BCP 185 and is not obsoleted. It is guidance for operators and is expected to evolve as deployment experience grows.

facts.label: Cache synchronisation
facts.value: At least every four to six hours

today: RFC 7115 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 185, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. The document says it is expected to evolve as RPKI-based origin validation continues to be deployed and the dynamics are better understood.

sections.title: What RPKI Origin Validation Is For
sections.content:
RPKI-based origin validation relies on widespread deployment of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). How the RPKI is distributed and maintained globally is a serious concern from many aspects. While the global RPKI is in the early stages of deployment, there is no single root trust anchor, initial testing is being done by the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), and there are technical testbeds. It is thought that origin validation based on the RPKI will continue to be deployed incrementally over the next few years, and it is assumed that eventually there must be a single root trust anchor for the public address space.

Origin validation needs to be done only by an AS's border routers, and is designed so that it can be used to protect announcements originated by any network participating in Internet BGP routing: large providers, upstream and downstream routers, and edge networks such as small stub or enterprise networks. It has been designed to be deployed on current routers without significant hardware upgrades, and should be used in border routers by operators from large backbones to small stub, enterprise and edge networks.

RPKI-based origin validation has been designed so that, with prudent local routing policies, there is little risk that what is seen as today's normal Internet routing is threatened by imprudent deployment of the global RPKI.

The document assumes the reader understands BGP, the RPKI, the RPKI Repository Structure, Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), the RPKI to Router Protocol, RPKI-based Prefix Validation and Ghostbusters Records.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple: address holders publish a signed record saying which network is allowed to announce their address space, and border routers check announcements against those records. The hard part is operating it, and this document is about that part.

sections.title: Assumed Background
sections.content:
The document assumes familiarity with the machinery the operational advice depends on. BGP is the routing protocol that carries the announcements. The RPKI is the infrastructure of signed certificates that ties an autonomous system number to the address space it is entitled to announce. The RPKI Repository Structure describes how the certificates, revocation lists, manifests and authorizations are laid out in a hierarchy of repositories.

Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) are the signed statements that say an autonomous system may originate a prefix; they are the objects origin validation actually consults. The RPKI to Router Protocol is how a validated cache feeds its data to a router, and RPKI-based Prefix Validation is the algorithm that turns a cache into one of three answers for a given announcement. Ghostbusters Records are the objects that carry contact information for the holder of a repository, so that a problem can be reported to the person who can fix it.

None of these is defined here. The document uses them as fixed points and concentrates on the operational questions: where the data comes from, how fresh it is, and how the answer should change routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: This section is a reading list rather than an explanation. It names the other documents that define the certificate format, the repository layout, the protocol that feeds routers and the check itself, so the rest of the document can talk about running the whole thing.

sections.title: Distributing and Maintaining the RPKI
sections.content:
The RPKI is a distributed database containing certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), manifests, ROAs and Ghostbusters Records. The RPKI repository design anticipated a hierarchic organization of repositories, as this seriously improves the performance of relying parties that gather data over a non-hierarchic organization, so publishing parties must implement hierarchic directory structures.

A local relying party's valid cache containing all RPKI data may be gathered from the global distributed database using the rsync protocol and a validation tool such as rcynic. A validated cache contains all the RPKI objects that the relying party has verified to be valid according to the rules for validating RPKI certificates and signed objects; entities that trust the cache can use these objects without further validation. Validated caches may also be created and maintained from other validated caches, and network operators should take maximum advantage of this feature to minimize the load on the global distributed RPKI database, with the recipient relying parties re-validating the data. As Trust Anchor Locators are critical to the RPKI trust model, operators should be very careful in their initial selection and vigilant in their maintenance.

To relieve routers of the load of performing certificate validation and cryptographic operations, the RPKI-Router protocol does not provide object-based security to the router: the router cannot validate the data cryptographically from a well-known trust anchor, trusts the cache to provide correct data, and relies on transport-based security for the data received from the cache. The authenticity and integrity of the data from the cache should therefore be well protected.

Operators should locate RPKI caches close to the routers that require the data, to minimize the impact of likely failures in local routing, intermediate devices and long circuits, and should consider trust boundaries and routing bootstrap reachability. A router should bootstrap from a cache reachable with minimal reliance on other infrastructure such as DNS or routing protocols, and configurations where the router needs its BGP or IGP to converge in order to reach the cache should be avoided if reasonably possible. If insecure transports are used between an operator's cache and its routers, the transport security recommendations of RFC 6810 should be followed, and operators must not use insecure transports between their routers and RPKI caches located in other Autonomous Systems. For redundancy, a router should peer with more than one cache at the same time, at least one local and others remote. An operator that trusts upstreams to carry its traffic may also trust the RPKI data those upstreams cache and should peer with the caches made available by them, which places an obligation on those upstreams to maintain fresh and reliable caches.

Before issuing a ROA for a super-block, an operator must ensure that all sub-allocations from that block announced by other ASes have correct ROAs in the RPKI, because otherwise the announcements of sub-allocations with no ROAs will be viewed as Invalid. While waiting for the recipients of sub-allocations to register ROAs, the owner of the super-block may use live BGP data to populate ROAs as a proxy.

ROAs should be as precise as possible, matching prefixes as announced in BGP, and software and operators should avoid excessive max length values unless operationally necessary. One advantage of minimal ROA length is that the forged origin attack does not work for sub-prefixes that are not covered by an overly long max length: if, instead of 10.0.0.0/16-24, one issues 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.42.0/24, a forged origin attack cannot succeed against 10.0.666.0/24, because the attacker must attack the whole /16, which is more likely to be noticed because of its size. ROA generation software must therefore use the prefix length as the max length if the user does not specify one. Operators should be conservative in the use of max length, and if a prefix is legitimately announced by more than one AS, ROAs for all of those ASes should be issued so that all are considered Valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is collected into a local cache that has already been checked, and routers read from that cache rather than doing cryptography themselves, so the link to the cache has to be protected. Publish your address space as narrowly as you can: a ROA that covers too much makes it easy to hijack a small piece of it without anyone noticing.

sections.title: Within a Network
sections.content:
Origin validation need only be done by edge routers in a network, those which border other networks or ASes. A validating router uses the result of origin validation to influence local policy within its network. In deployment this policy should fit into the AS's existing policy and preferences, which allows a network to incrementally deploy validation-capable border routers.

The operator should be aware that RPKI-based origin validation, as any other policy change, can cause traffic shifts in their network, and that as with normal policy shift practice, a prudent operator has tools and methods to predict, measure and modify the effect.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the routers at the edge of your network need to validate. Because validation changes what the routers prefer, traffic can move, so the change should be introduced gradually and watched.

sections.title: Turning Validation into Routing Policy
sections.content:
Origin validation based on the RPKI marks a received announcement as having an origin that is Valid, NotFound or Invalid. How this is used in routing should be specified by the operator's local policy.

Local policy using relative preference is suggested to manage the uncertainty associated with a system in early deployment, and can eliminate the threat of unreachability of prefixes due to ill-advised certification policies or incorrect certification data. Until the community feels comfortable relying on RPKI data, routing on Invalid origin validity, though at a low preference, may occur. Operators should be aware that accepting Invalid announcements, no matter how de-preferenced, will often be the equivalent of treating them as fully Valid: consider a ROA for AS 42 for prefix 10.0.0.0/16-24, where a BGP announcement for 10.0.666.0/24 from AS 666 would be Invalid, but if policy is not configured to discard it then longest-match forwarding will send packets toward AS 666, no matter the value of local preference.

As origin validation is rolled out incrementally, coverage will be incomplete for a long time, so routing on the NotFound validity state should be done for a long time. An operator's policy should not be overly strict: it should prefer Valid announcements, attach a lower preference to but still use NotFound announcements, and drop or give a very low preference to Invalid announcements. Merely de-preferencing Invalid announcements is ill-advised.

Some providers may choose to set Local-Preference based on the RPKI validation result. Others may not want the validation result to be more important than AS_PATH length, and would need to map it to some BGP attribute that is evaluated in the path selection process after the AS_PATH is evaluated; routers implementing RPKI-based origin validation must provide such options to operators. Local-Preference may be used to carry both the validity state of a prefix along with its traffic engineering characteristics, and an operator already using Local-Preference will have to change policy so that these two characteristics are encoded in the same attribute without negative impact or opening privilege escalation attacks; for example, validation state should not be encoded in higher bits than those used for traffic engineering. When using a metric that is also influenced by other local policy, an operator should be careful not to create privilege-upgrade vulnerabilities: if Local Pref is set depending on validity state, peer community signaling should not upgrade an Invalid announcement to Valid or better.

Announcements with Valid origins should be preferred over those with NotFound or Invalid origins, if Invalid origins are accepted at all. Announcements with NotFound origins should be preferred over those with Invalid origins. Announcements with Invalid origins should not be used, but may be used to meet special operational needs, in which case they should have a lower preference than Valid or NotFound. When first deploying origin validation, it may be prudent not to drop announcements with Invalid origins until inspection of logs, SNMP or other data indicates that the correct result would be obtained. Validity state signaling should not be accepted from a neighbor AS, since the validity state of a received announcement has only local scope, because of issues such as scope of trust, RPKI synchrony and management of local trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three answers and three rules for them. Valid wins. NotFound, meaning nobody has published a record, stays usable for a long time with a lower preference, because coverage is still incomplete. Invalid, meaning the announcement contradicts a published record, is dropped, and just giving it a low preference is not enough because the longest-prefix match still sends the traffic there.

sections.title: Operational Notes and Recommendations
sections.content:
Like DNS, the global RPKI presents only a loosely consistent view, depending on timing, updating and fetching, so one cache or router may have different data about a particular prefix than another. There is no fix for this; it is the nature of distributed data with distributed caches. Operators should beware that RPKI caches are loosely synchronized, even within a single AS, so changes to the validity state of prefixes could differ within an operator's network, and there is no guaranteed interval from when a cache is updated to when the new information reaches the routers. This may result in sudden shifts of traffic until all of the routers in the AS have reached equilibrium.

There is some uncertainty about the origin AS of aggregates and what, if any, ROA can be used; the long-range solution is the deprecation of AS_SETs. Since reliable access to the global RPKI and to an operator's caches is important, an operator should take advantage of relying-party tools that report changes in BGP or RPKI data that would negatively affect validation of such prefixes.

Operators should be aware of a trade-off in the placement of an RPKI repository in address space for which the repository's content is authoritative: on one hand an operator wants to maximize control over the repository, and on the other hand, if there are reachability problems to that address space, changes in the repository to correct them may not be easily accessed by others. Operators who manage certificates should associate RPKI Ghostbusters Records with each publication point they control, which are the points holding the CRL, ROAs and other signed objects issued by the operator.

Routers that perform RPKI-based origin validation must support Four-octet AS Numbers, as it is not reasonable to generate ROAs for AS 23456. Software that produces filter lists for routers where the target router does not support four-octet AS numbers must be prepared to accept them and generate the appropriate two-octet output. As a router must evaluate certificates and ROAs that are time dependent, routers' clocks must be correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour, and servers should provide time service such as NTPv4 to client routers.

Operators using RPKI data as an input to operational routing decisions should ensure local caches inside their AS are synchronized with each other at least every four to six hours, and should use tools that warn them of any impending ROA or certificate expiry that could affect the validity of their own data; Ghostbusters Records can be used to facilitate contact with upstream Certification Authorities to effect repair.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical warnings. The data is never perfectly in step between caches, so traffic can shift as one cache catches up with another. The certificates have expiry dates, so something has to watch them. And the router's clock has to be right, because the certificates are checked against the time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: As the BGP origin AS of an update is not signed, origin validation is open to malicious spoofing, and RPKI-based origin validation is therefore expected to deal only with inadvertent mis-advertisement. Origin validation does not address the problem of AS_PATH validation, so paths are open to manipulation, either malicious or accidental. As BGP does not ensure that traffic will flow via the paths it advertises, the data plane may not follow the control plane. The class of privilege escalation issues discussed in Section 5 should also be kept in mind.
sections.plainLanguage: What this catches is a network announcing addresses it was not given by mistake. It does not catch a deliberate hijack, because the announcement itself carries no signature, and it says nothing about the path the traffic takes.

messages.label: RPKI objects
messages.note: Certificates, CRLs, manifests, ROAs and Ghostbusters Records, gathered with rsync.

messages.label: Validated cache
messages.note: Caches can be built from other validated caches, which reduces the load on the global database.

messages.label: RPKI-Router protocol
messages.note: The router trusts the cache and relies on transport security; it does no cryptography itself.

items.label: An authorized origin exists
items.desc: Prefer these announcements over everything else.

items.label: No authorized origin is known
items.desc: Still use these, with a lower preference than Valid, for a long time.

items.label: The origin is not authorized
items.desc: Drop them, or give them a very low preference; merely de-preferencing them does not work.

items.title: Clock accuracy
items.text: Router clocks must be correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour.

items.title: Cache synchronisation
items.text: Local caches should be synchronised with each other at least every four to six hours.

items.title: Expiry warnings
items.text: Use tools that warn about impending ROA or certificate expiry.

items.title: Ghostbusters Records
items.text: Associate them with each publication point so a problem can be reported.

items.title: Four-octet AS numbers
items.text: Routers doing validation must support them; ROAs are not generated for AS 23456.

items.title: Loose consistency
items.text: Caches are never perfectly in step, so traffic can shift as they catch up.
